question: What is the risk level of my AI-powered personnel recruitment SaaS platform (which performs automatic CV pre-screening and candidate performance prediction) under the EU AI Act?
gold_answer: Under the EU AI Act, the AI-powered recruitment platform qualifies as a high-risk AI system pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 4(a), because it is used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, in particular to analyse and filter job applications and to evaluate candidates, which significantly impacts access to employment.

question: What specific regulatory obligations must my organization comply with based on the EU AI Act for this high-risk recruitment AI system?
gold_answer: As a provider of a high-risk recruitment AI system, the organization must implement a continuous risk management system (Article 9), ensure data governance and bias mitigation (Article 10), draw up comprehensive technical documentation (Article 11 and Annex IV), maintain automated logging (Article 12), ensure transparency and instructions for use (Article 13), enable human oversight with override capabilities (Article 14), ensure accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity (Article 15), conduct a conformity assessment with CE marking (Articles 43 and 48), and establish post-market monitoring (Article 72).

question: What are the potential legal risks associated with this AI recruitment tool, and what compliance measures must be implemented to mitigate these risks?
gold_answer: The primary legal risks include violation of fundamental rights regarding non-discrimination and equality (Article 21 of the EU Charter; Article 10 of the AI Act) through unrepresentative training datasets, unlawful automated decision-making lacking human oversight (Article 14 AI Act; Article 22 GDPR), and severe regulatory fines under Article 99. Mandatory mitigations include dataset bias audits, continuous human intervention protocols, and fundamental rights risk mapping.

question: Which areas of the recruitment AI system are not yet compliant with applicable regulatory obligations when bias audits, formal risk management, and decision logging are missing?
gold_answer: The system presents critical compliance gaps under Article 9 (absence of a formal lifecycle risk management system), Article 10 (lack of bias detection audits and representative data governance), Article 12 (absence of automated logging and audit traceability), Article 14 (inadequate human oversight and override mechanisms), and Article 11 (missing technical file). These gaps require establishing documented risk procedures, statistical bias testing, tamper-proof logging, and human supervisor controls.

question: What mandatory technical documentation is required to demonstrate compliance with the EU AI Act for this recruitment tool, and what specific documents must be prepared?
gold_answer: Article 11(1) requires technical documentation that demonstrates conformity with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements and contains, at a minimum, the nine elements set out in Annex IV: (1) a general description of the recruitment system, its intended purpose, versions, interfaces and the hardware it runs on; (2) a detailed description of its development, including the design specifications and general logic of the algorithms, the system architecture (point 2(c)), datasheets on the training data sets and their provenance and labelling procedures (point 2(d)), the assessment of the human oversight measures needed under Article 14 (point 2(e)), the validation and testing procedures with the metrics used to measure accuracy, robustness and potentially discriminatory impacts (point 2(g)), and the cybersecurity measures (point 2(h)); (3) information on monitoring, functioning and control, including the degrees of accuracy for specific groups of candidates and the foreseeable risks of discrimination; (4) a description of the appropriateness of the performance metrics; (5) a detailed description of the risk management system under Article 9; (6) a description of relevant lifecycle changes; (7) the list of harmonised standards applied; (8) a copy of the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47, whose content is specified in Annex V; and (9) a description of the post-market monitoring system and plan under Article 72. The Article 10 data governance and bias audit records are documented through points 2(d) and 2(g). CE marking is not an Annex IV element: it is affixed separately under Article 48 after the Article 43 conformity assessment.

question: What is the risk level of an AI system used in hospitals for medical diagnosis, treatment recommendations, patient triage, and survival prediction under the EU AI Act?
gold_answer: The medical diagnostic and triage AI system qualifies as a high-risk AI system under Article 6(1) in conjunction with Annex I (as a safety component of a medical device subject to third-party conformity assessment under MDR 2017/745) and Article 6(2) regarding essential healthcare triage.

question: What specific regulatory obligations must be met for this AI medical diagnostic and triage system under the EU AI Act?
gold_answer: The provider must implement a risk management system integrated with ISO 14971 (Article 9), high-quality clinical data governance (Article 10), technical documentation aligned with MDR Annex II/III (Article 11, Annex IV), event logging (Article 12), clinical transparency and user manuals (Article 13), clinician human oversight to prevent automation bias (Article 14), accuracy and cybersecurity resilience (Article 15), joint notified body conformity assessment (Article 43(3)), and dual-track incident reporting (Article 73 for AI Act; MDR Article 87 for medical vigilance).

question: What are the legal risks associated with using AI survival modeling and lifestyle-based triage in hospital care?
gold_answer: Key legal risks involve violations of human dignity and the right to healthcare non-discrimination (EU Charter Articles 1, 21, and 35; AI Act Article 10), automation bias where doctors over-rely on automated triage without critical review (Article 14), unlawful processing of special category health data (GDPR Article 9; AI Act Article 10(5)), and civil/product liability in case of diagnostic failure.

question: What compliance gaps arise if the medical diagnostic AI lacks physician override controls and clinical dataset validation across diverse demographics?
gold_answer: Major gaps exist under Article 10(2) due to unrepresentative demographic datasets causing diagnostic disparities, Article 14 due to missing doctor override and stop mechanisms, Article 11 due to incomplete clinical validation files in technical documentation, and Article 72 due to absent post-market clinical follow-up.

question: What technical documentation must be prepared for an AI medical diagnostic system to satisfy EU AI Act Article 11 and Annex IV requirements?
gold_answer: Article 11(1) requires technical documentation containing, at a minimum, the nine elements set out in Annex IV: (1) a general description of the diagnostic system, its intended purpose, versions and the hardware it runs on; (2) a detailed description of its development, including the design specifications and general logic of the algorithms, the system architecture and computational resources (point 2(c)), datasheets on the clinical training data sets and their provenance (point 2(d)), the assessment of the clinician human oversight measures needed under Article 14 (point 2(e)), the validation and testing procedures and accuracy, robustness and discriminatory-impact metrics with dated test logs (point 2(g)), and the cybersecurity measures (point 2(h)); (3) information on monitoring, functioning and control, including the degrees of accuracy for specific patient groups; (4) a description of the appropriateness of the performance metrics; (5) a detailed description of the ISO 14971-aligned risk management system under Article 9; (6) a description of relevant lifecycle changes; (7) the list of harmonised standards applied; (8) a copy of the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47; and (9) a description of the post-market monitoring system and plan under Article 72, which for a medical device is run jointly with MDR post-market clinical follow-up. CE marking is not an Annex IV element: it is affixed separately under Article 48 following the Article 43 conformity assessment.

question: What is the risk level of an AI-based intelligent traffic management system that dynamically controls city traffic lights based on live camera feeds and IoT sensors under the EU AI Act?
gold_answer: The intelligent traffic management system is classified as a high-risk AI system pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 2, as it is used as a safety component in the management and operation of road traffic. Annex III point 2 is a single unlettered paragraph covering critical digital infrastructure, road traffic and the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity; there is no point 2(a).

question: What regulatory obligations apply to a municipal operator deploying an AI-powered road traffic management system under the EU AI Act?
gold_answer: The provider and deployer must maintain a continuous risk management system against physical safety hazards (Article 9), ensure training data quality for camera vision models (Article 10), compile technical documentation (Article 11 and Annex IV), provide the automatic event logging capability (Article 12) and retain the deployer logs for at least six months (Article 26(6)), ensure human traffic operators can override signals (Article 14), safeguard cybersecurity against remote tampering (Article 15), and comply with deployer operational oversight duties (Article 26).

question: What legal and fundamental rights risks arise from using computer vision cameras and vehicle tracking in municipal traffic AI systems?
gold_answer: Primary legal risks include mass surveillance and privacy infringements under Article 8 of the EU Charter and GDPR if vehicle license plates or facial images are captured without effective anonymization, critical safety failures causing physical traffic accidents (Article 9), and civil liability for infrastructure disruption.

question: What compliance gaps exist if a smart traffic AI system lacks fail-safe fallback modes and cyberattack resilience testing?
gold_answer: The system suffers from critical gaps under Article 15 (failure to demonstrate robustness against sensor faults and cyber-attacks), Article 9 (incomplete risk evaluation for emergency vehicle routing failures), Article 14 (lack of manual override protocols for traffic operators), and Article 12 (insufficient event logging during traffic anomalies).

question: What technical documentation must be established for an intelligent traffic management AI system under Article 11 and Annex IV of the EU AI Act?
gold_answer: Article 11(1) requires technical documentation containing, at a minimum, the nine elements set out in Annex IV: (1) a general description of the traffic management system, its intended purpose, versions and the IoT sensor and camera hardware it runs on; (2) a detailed description of its development, including the design specifications and general logic of the algorithms, the system architecture (point 2(c)), datasheets on the training data sets (point 2(d)), the assessment of the human operator oversight measures needed under Article 14 (point 2(e)), the validation and testing procedures with sensor error rates and accuracy and robustness metrics (point 2(g)), and the cybersecurity measures against remote tampering (point 2(h), giving effect to Article 15); (3) information on monitoring, functioning and control, including foreseeable unintended outcomes and sources of risk to health and safety; (4) a description of the appropriateness of the performance metrics; (5) a detailed description of the risk management system covering infrastructure safety under Article 9; (6) a description of relevant lifecycle changes; (7) the list of harmonised standards applied; (8) a copy of the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47; and (9) a description of the post-market monitoring system and plan under Article 72. The file must also evidence the Article 12 automatic event logging capability; Article 12 itself sets no log retention period, and the provider must keep those logs for at least six months under Article 19(1). CE marking is not an Annex IV element: it is affixed separately under Article 48.

question: What is the risk level of an in-store AI system using facial recognition for VIP matching, theft alerts against flagged images, and behavioral gaze analysis under the EU AI Act?
gold_answer: The system spans multiple regulatory tiers: real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces is prohibited under Article 5(1)(h) when conducted by law enforcement; biometric categorization for retail profiling is classified as high-risk under Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 1; emotion or interest recognition requires mandatory transparency disclosure to consumers under Article 50(3).

question: What obligations must a retail store fulfill when deploying AI facial recognition and behavioral analytics?
gold_answer: The deployer must first verify that the system does not fall under the Article 5 prohibitions, then discharge the Article 26 deployer obligations: use the system in accordance with the instructions for use and assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence and authority (Article 26(1)-(2), giving effect to Article 14), meet the Article 50(3) transparency duty by clearly informing exposed individuals of the biometric and emotion analysis, inform affected persons that they are subject to a high-risk AI system (Article 26(11)), ensure a valid lawful basis — in retail, in practice explicit consent — for processing biometric data (GDPR Article 9), and observe the six-month log retention floor for the logs it controls (Article 26(6)). An Article 27 fundamental rights impact assessment is NOT required of this deployer: Article 27(1) reaches only deployers that are bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, and deployers of Annex III point 5(b) or (c) systems, and a private retail chain operating an Annex III point 1 biometric system is none of those.

question: What legal risks arise from using retail facial recognition for theft alerting and dynamic behavior-based pricing?
gold_answer: Severe legal risks include: (1) prohibited creation or expansion of a facial recognition database through the untargeted scraping of facial images from CCTV footage, if the flagged-image watchlist is built that way (Article 5(1)(e)); (2) prohibited social scoring, if the behaviour-based pricing evaluates customers over a period of time on their behaviour or personality characteristics and the resulting score leads to unfavourable treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate, or that occurs in a social context unrelated to the one in which the data was collected (Article 5(1)(c)); (3) racial, gender, or demographic bias in facial matching algorithms violating Article 21 of the EU Charter and the Article 10 data governance duty; (4) unlawful processing of biometric data without valid explicit consent under GDPR Article 9; and (5) maximum regulatory penalties of up to 35 million EUR or 7% of global annual turnover under Article 99(3). Article 5(1)(h) is not engaged: the real-time remote biometric identification prohibition applies to use for the purposes of law enforcement, which a retail chain is not conducting.

question: What compliance gaps exist if retail facial recognition is deployed without signage, without a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment, and automated theft alerts trigger security interventions without human confirmation?
gold_answer: Critical deficiencies include violation of Article 50(3) (failure to provide conspicuous transparency notices to shoppers exposed to biometric categorisation and emotion recognition), the Article 26(11) deployer obligation (failure to inform affected persons that they are subject to a high-risk AI system), Article 14 (lack of meaningful human oversight before security actions), and Article 10 (unverified accuracy and demographic false-positive rates on facial recognition). The absence of a fundamental rights impact assessment is NOT a compliance gap here: Article 27(1) imposes that assessment only on deployers that are bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, or deployers of Annex III point 5(b) or (c) systems, so it does not reach a private retail chain running an Annex III point 1 biometric system. Note also that Article 27(3) requires notification of the assessment results to the market surveillance authority, not registration.

question: What technical documentation is required for high-risk biometric identification and retail analytics systems under the EU AI Act?
gold_answer: Article 11(1) requires the provider's technical documentation to contain, at a minimum, the nine elements set out in Annex IV: (1) a general description of the biometric system, its intended purpose, versions and hardware; (2) a detailed description of its development, including the design specifications and general logic of the facial feature extraction and CNN models, the system architecture (point 2(c)), datasheets on the training data sets and their provenance and labelling (point 2(d)), the assessment of the human oversight measures needed under Article 14 for security staff (point 2(e)), the validation and testing procedures with false match rate (FMR) and false non-match rate (FNMR) benchmarks across demographic cohorts and potentially discriminatory impacts (point 2(g), giving effect to Article 15), and the cybersecurity measures (point 2(h)); (3) information on monitoring, functioning and control, including the degrees of accuracy for specific groups of persons; (4) a description of the appropriateness of the performance metrics; (5) a detailed description of the risk management system under Article 9; (6) a description of relevant lifecycle changes; (7) the list of harmonised standards applied; (8) a copy of the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47; and (9) a description of the post-market monitoring system and plan under Article 72. Three items commonly listed here are NOT Annex IV elements: CE marking is affixed separately under Article 48; the six-month log retention floor sits in Article 19(1) for the provider and Article 26(6) for the deployer, not in Article 12, which states only the logging capability; and an Article 27 fundamental rights impact assessment is not part of the technical file and is in any event not required of a private retail deployer of an Annex III point 1 system.
